video_title: Lawfare Daily: The Trump-Xi Summit and U.S.-China AI Competition
gist: Peterson Institute fellow Martin (guest) tells Peter Harrell that US-China ties after the Sept. 24 Trump-Xi summit are a fragile rare-earths-vs-chips stalemate, with the MATCH Act (forcing ASML to stop servicing Chinese tools) the key escalation risk. He explains why China is refusing permitted Nvidia chips (Huawei vs. labs), shares tests showing censorship and fabrication baked into DeepSeek and Kimi weights even when hosted in the US, and argues renminbi internationalization has stalled (~28% of China trade in RMB).

themes.theme: Rare earths vs chips strategic stalemate

insights.claim: The core of the US-China tech relationship is a strategic stalemate between China's rare earth leverage and US technology sales, with asymmetric desires: the US wants as many rare earths as possible while trying to reduce dependence, whereas China does not want as many US chips as the US is willing to sell.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Chip export loosening does not translate into proportional China demand; rare earth supply remains the binding US vulnerability.
insights.quote: the biggest one is the overall strategic stalemate between the rare earth issue and then a wide suite of other tech that the US sells to China

insights.claim: The US has loosened chip export controls without China offering anything in exchange, because Beijing fears that importing US chips would hurt its semiconductor indigenization drive.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Limits upside for US chip vendors' China revenue even under permissive licensing.

insights.claim: In the near term, mutual economic coercion capacity is contributing to stability: China's rare earth retaliation against escalating Trump tariffs forced the US to pull back, and fear of China 'pressing that button again' has led the executive branch to push back on congressional China initiatives likely to provoke retaliation.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Executive branch is a brake on hawkish legislation; policy risk rises if that restraint weakens.
insights.quote: the fear of China pressing that button again has led to for example the executive branch pushing back on all sorts of congressional initiatives

insights.claim: Chinese interlocutors are pessimistic long term, view Trump as an aberration from the bipartisan hawkish consensus, and are unwilling to make concessions that assume the current period of relative peace will last.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Expect transactional, reversible deals rather than durable structural agreements.

insights.claim: The US side reportedly did not want to simply extend the rare earth truce on current terms, so rare earths will remain a point of frustration heading into the APEC and G20 meetings.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Rare earth supply terms remain an open, negotiable risk for defense and industrial supply chains.

insights.claim: Upcoming Trump-Xi encounters at APEC and the G20 (Xi visiting the US later this winter) are the next windows to watch for AI dialogue, rare earth terms, and the MATCH Act's fate.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell (host)
insights.so_what: Event calendar for US-China policy catalysts.

themes.theme: MATCH Act and ASML escalation risk

insights.claim: The MATCH Act, which has a decent chance of passing, would require the Netherlands and other semiconductor-equipment nations to match US export controls and would tangibly force ASML to stop servicing machines already deployed in China.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Direct risk to ASML's China installed-base service revenue and a major escalation trigger.
insights.quote: This is something that has a decent chance of passing

insights.claim: China would view the MATCH Act as a major escalation because it moves from not selling to making inoperable equipment China has already bought — described as forcing the Dutch to 'brick' expensive machines.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Bricking installed tools is a qualitatively different escalation that could unlock severe Chinese retaliation.
insights.quote: you're going from not selling something to China to making inoperable something that has already been sold to China

insights.claim: A likely retaliation path to MATCH-style action is China reinstating extraterritorial rare earth controls modeled on the US foreign direct product rule and de minimis rules, asserting jurisdiction over any product containing even small amounts of Chinese rare earths, causing global supply chain snarls.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Tail risk for any manufacturer using Chinese-origin rare earths, globally, not just in the US.

insights.claim: The guest argues Americans fail to mirror China's logic: if the US restricts chips because they aid China's military and AI, China can equally argue that selling rare earths aids the US defense industrial base and AI ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Raises probability China treats rare earths as a strategic, not purely commercial, lever indefinitely.

insights.claim: If the House shifts after the midterms, hawkish China bills that have been stalled may begin to pass, which Chinese firms are watching closely.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Midterms are a regime-change risk for US-China economic policy.

insights.claim: The term 'overcapacity' originated in Chinese domestic discourse rather than as a Western accusation, according to the guest's etymological research.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Undercuts Beijing's framing that overcapacity is a Western invention, strengthening trade-remedy arguments.
insights.quote: I actually traced back the etmology of this and found that it's actually coming from Chinese domestic discourse

insights.claim: Chinese overcapacity persists because state-backed lenders and local governments, facing a continuing property contraction and weak economy, refuse to let failing factories close or recognize bad loans.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Structural deflationary export pressure from China is unlikely to self-correct.

insights.claim: Chinese property continues to shrink after many years of contraction, which remains a major drag on the Chinese economy.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Supports continued weak Chinese domestic demand and export push.

insights.claim: US tariffs insulate the US from Chinese overcapacity but exacerbate it for the rest of the world, as goods blocked from the US flow into third markets in greater quantities — visible in trade flow data.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Expect rising trade defense actions in Europe and other third markets.

insights.claim: Even if Trump allowed Chinese EV makers to sell US-built cars, Chinese automakers would likely hesitate because factories take years to build and a future president or hawkish Congress could reinstate a ban just as production starts.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Lowers probability of near-term Chinese auto FDI into the US, despite political noise.

insights.claim: China shifted from not retaliating against US controls in the early Biden years to retaliating and enforcing anti-sanctions blocking rules by the late Biden administration, driven by rising confidence and a view that the US is a bully who must be punched back.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: US sanctions on Chinese firms now carry higher retaliation risk for US companies.

insights.claim: Chinese interlocutors said in hindsight they should not have retaliated against Trump's first-term tariffs, believing it worsened relations, before later reversing to a punch-back stance.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Shows China's retaliation doctrine is adaptive and currently hawkish.

insights.claim: Being on the US Entity List became a fundraising asset in China, with firms using designation to raise money and win government assistance.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Entity listing can accelerate state support for targeted Chinese competitors rather than cripple them.
insights.quote: if you're not on the entity list, you're not doing anything interesting

insights.claim: China's use of rare earth controls around the Liberation Day tariffs, plus European companies begging for controlled minerals, convinced Beijing it holds a very powerful lever and is less lopsidedly dependent on the world.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Beijing will be quicker to deploy mineral controls in future disputes.

insights.claim: China likely believes the US will not use major financial sanctions against it because doing so would hurt the US too, and because the administration worries about dollar role and Treasury demand.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Treasury-market sensitivity constrains US financial coercion against China.
insights.quote: it's like throwing a a hand grenade that's going to explode before it gets fully out of your blast radius

insights.claim: The Trump administration has found it diplomatically easier to naval-blockade Venezuelan and then Iranian oil tankers bound for China than to sanction a large Chinese company in that trade, even though about 90% of Iranian oil flowed to China before the blockade.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell (host)
insights.so_what: Physical interdiction, not financial sanctions, is the live US tool on China-linked oil flows.
insights.quote: 90% of the oil was flow from Iran was flowing to China prior to the blockade

insights.claim: From his State Department Iran-sanctions experience, the host observed that successive sanctions rounds got politically easier, not harder, because business constituencies opposing them dried up as ties shrank.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell (host)
insights.so_what: Decoupling lowers the political cost of further sanctions — a key reason China avoids it.

themes.theme: US vs China AI regulation and frontier gap

insights.claim: China has more AI-specific regulation than the US — including generative AI service registration, mandatory labeling of AI-generated media, and recent rules on AI companions — but lacks frontier security review, so a Chinese lab can release a new model version without pre-release safety evaluation.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Chinese labs can ship faster than US labs now subject to security reviews.
insights.quote: China has much more AI specific regulation than the US

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic now need to go through a security review in the US before releasing new models, under what the host describes as a new White House voluntary framework.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Adds release friction and lag for US frontier labs.

insights.claim: US AI oversight remains unsettled, with options including CAISI under Commerce or a FINRA-type self-regulatory organization overseen by the SEC, reportedly proposed by Bessent.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Regulatory architecture for AI still in flux; SRO model would be industry-friendly.

insights.claim: The public gap between US and Chinese models may be as small as 4-6 months, but the gap between the best internal models at US and Chinese labs is much greater, with recent US models showing acceleration in recursive self-improvement.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Public benchmark parity understates the US frontier lead.
insights.quote: even if the public gap is something like 6 months or as low as 4 months the gap between the best internal models at Chinese labs and the best internal models at US labs is much greater

insights.claim: Chinese labs are less worried about frontier risk because they are not at the frontier, do less compute-expensive red-teaming, regulate reactively rather than ex ante, lack an effective-altruism-style safety ecosystem, and are more skeptical LLMs lead to AGI.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Low odds of a binding US-China AI safety regime soon.

insights.claim: China distrusts US calls for AI safety pacing because it sees US export controls as having already paced China away from the frontier.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Limits scope of AI hotline/dialogue outcomes.

insights.claim: A realistic near-term AI goal is working-level US-China talks on preventing escalation if an AI system breaches the other side's government or infrastructure, though the Trump administration is divided on talking to China about AI safety.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: AI diplomacy outcomes will likely be modest confidence-building measures.

themes.theme: China compute constraints and chip politics

insights.claim: China's refusal to buy permitted Nvidia chips reflects a split: Chinese AI labs want Nvidia chips and the CUDA ecosystem to compete, while Huawei lobbies the government that domestic supply is sufficient and imports perpetuate dependence.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Nvidia China sales depend on Beijing's internal politics, not just US licensing.

insights.claim: Huawei's Ren Zhengfei told Xi Jinping directly that Huawei can supply far more and its constraints have eased, arguing against letting labs buy foreign chips.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Huawei has top-level influence pushing China away from Nvidia.

insights.claim: DeepSeek attempted to move training to Huawei chips and had to delay its next model release.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Domestic Chinese chips still impose real costs on frontier training.

insights.claim: DeepSeek's head complained a few months ago of having 16,000 Huawei chips, roughly equivalent to 4,000 two-year-old US chips, while US clusters now treat 100,000 far more powerful chips as a bare minimum.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the large China compute deficit.
insights.quote: 16,000 Huawei chips, which is equivalent to like 4,000 US chips from 2 years ago

insights.claim: Chinese labs' pleas for imports are undermined by US alarm over how close Chinese models are, letting Beijing tell them to buy Huawei chips instead.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: US 'China is catching up' narratives can paradoxically hurt Nvidia's China demand.

insights.claim: Remote access to chips in data centers abroad, particularly in Southeast Asia, is a legal escape valve for Chinese firms; export controls do not easily cover services, and either side could shut it off.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian data center demand partly rests on a regulatory loophole that could close.

insights.claim: The US corporate divide mirrors China's: in the US chipmakers want to sell to China while labs oppose it; in China labs want to buy while domestic chipmakers oppose imports.
insights.speaker: Peter Harrell (host)
insights.so_what: Useful map of lobbying forces on chip export policy.

themes.theme: Hidden behaviors in Chinese open-weight models

insights.claim: Testing Chinese open-weight models served from a US provider on a politically sensitive scandal produced divergent results: GLM answered fully, Kimi gave propaganda then corrected itself after self-criticism, and DeepSeek doubled down and fabricated sources.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Censorship can be baked into weights, so self-hosting does not neutralize Chinese-model risk.

insights.claim: DeepSeek falsely claimed Bloomberg had recanted its reporting and fabricated BBC and Reuters articles with broken links, then offered Wayback Machine links, suggesting possible training data poisoning.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Raises latent-behavior and reliability concerns for enterprises deploying DeepSeek.
insights.quote: maybe they poisoned the training data

insights.claim: Open weights are not transparent: no engineer can read billions of weights to detect encoded behaviors, so each new Chinese model version needs rigorous testing before adoption.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Model-evaluation and AI-assurance tooling has an emerging market.

insights.claim: The guest opposes banning Chinese open-weight models, warning that a unilateral US ban would be an AIIB-style diplomatic fiasco that no other countries would follow, absent a smoking gun.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Lowers probability of a near-term US ban on Chinese open models.
insights.quote: I don't think there's any smoking gun that anyone's found yet that would justify a full ban

insights.claim: Cheap, commoditized open models shift AI returns from labs to AI users, so banning cost-competitive Chinese models would disadvantage US AI-using firms, which is why Silicon Valley and VCs oppose open-weight restrictions.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Model commoditization compresses lab margins and benefits application-layer companies.
insights.quote: that shifts the returns away from the labs and towards the users of AI

insights.claim: The renminbi's share of SWIFT payments rose from about 2.5% to just under 5% after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, briefly ranking fourth, but has since fallen back to around sixth, behind the Canadian dollar.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: De-dollarization via RMB is stalling, not accelerating.

insights.claim: Only about 28% of China's trade is denominated in renminbi, and roughly 90% of the rest is in US dollars, so China remains heavily dollar-dependent.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Dollar leverage over China remains substantial.
insights.quote: only about 28% of China's trade is currently denominated in the remn

insights.claim: RMB internationalization is capped mainly by China's closed capital account and prioritization of currency stability over opening.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: No major RMB breakout expected absent capital account liberalization.

insights.claim: The RMB decline is real, driven partly by lower FDI into China and low Chinese bond yields that make RMB attractive for borrowing but not investing.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Weak foreign appetite for RMB assets is a structural headwind.

insights.claim: The dollar functions as a hub because thin bilateral currency markets make direct exchange costly; Korea had no direct won-renminbi conversion until about 2017.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Network effects entrench dollar dominance.

insights.claim: China's CIPS system, about 10 years old and initially integrated with SWIFT, is expanding direct participants as insurance against SWIFT exclusion.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: CIPS is a contingency rail, not a dollar replacement.

insights.claim: Chinese thinkers concluded that 'fortress Russia' decoupling lowered the cost of sanctions, so China integrates more deeply into global finance as mutually assured destruction.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: China will stay financially intertwined, raising costs of sanctioning it.

insights.claim: China's $50,000 annual limit on taking money out also applies to bringing money in, forcing special channels for tax repatriation.
insights.speaker: Martin (guest, Peterson Institute senior fellow)
insights.so_what: Shows how restrictive China's capital account remains.
